The trade-off is resolved by the real-time-versus-offline boundary and the safety hierarchy: deterministic functions live below, intelligent ones above, and the interface between them is a contract in which intelligence proposes and determinism disposes. Neither property is compromised, because neither is asked to do the other's job.
Why not one or the other

A purely deterministic plant could not reason about a coupled nonlinear plasma fast enough to run efficiently; a purely intelligent one could not guarantee the microsecond response the magnets demand. The architecture is the argument that you can have both — but only if you keep them apart and wire them together through contracts.
This split defines the real-time versus offline boundary and orders the safety hierarchy.

title: From Diagnostics to Decision
lede: One trace up the stack: how a raw diagnostic sample becomes a validated feature, a twin state, a prediction, and a bounded action.
body: The clearest way to understand the architecture is to follow a single measurement from the machine to an action and back. This trace ties the layers, colors, and line semantics together in one path.
A Thomson-scattering sample crosses a cryo-rated feedthrough into L2 (blue).
L2 validates, normalizes, and feature-engineers it, recording lineage.
GNNs fuse it with the constellation and impute any dropped neighbors.
PINNs update the twin's equilibrium (breeder) or potential (burner) estimate.
The twin projects the state 50-100 ms ahead; anomaly ensembles score it.

If the forecast approaches a limit — a disruption boundary on the breeder, a plug-density floor on the burner — the MPC agent (yellow) plans a corrective trajectory over the twin. The trajectory is a proposal, not a command. It carries the twin state and lineage that justify it.
L4's rules engine checks the trajectory against safety bounds (purple/gray).
If accepted, L1 executes it deterministically within the command boundary (orange path).
If the model is uncertain or the bound is violated, the plant falls back to conservative control.
The outcome is archived; any surprise becomes a pink signal for retraining.

This is the whole architecture in miniature: telemetry rising, authority descending, intelligence proposing, determinism disposing, and the loop closing through feedback. It combines the layer connections with the line semantics and the color grammar.

title: Reading the Blueprint
lede: A practical guide to reading any Master Blueprint diagram: check the layer, the color, the line, and the termination — in that order.
body: How to read a blueprint diagram
The Master Blueprint diagrams pack a great deal into a single page. Read in a fixed order, they are unambiguous. This guide is the order Kronos engineers use.
Which layer? Find the horizontal band — L0 at the bottom to L7 at the top — to know the role and latency class.
Which color? The block's color gives its function — governance, infrastructure, operations, AI, reactor, feedback, or framing.
Which line? The connection style gives the latency class — microsecond real-time, standard telemetry, or offline batch.
Which termination? Follow the block to the named subsystem it touches — a magnet, a feedthrough, the divertor, the DEC train.

Reading in this order makes violations pop out. A pink block on the sub-10-microsecond path (a feedback function on the safety line) is wrong. A standard-telemetry line touching the command boundary is wrong. A yellow AI block wired straight to an orange actuator without passing through a purple/gray safety gate is wrong. The grammar is designed so that mistakes look like mistakes.

The same reading order works for the breeder and burner blueprints. Because the lower layers are shared, only the L3-and-above blocks and the reactor terminations change: a spherical torus and shaping coils for Hyperion, an open mirror and plug coils for the burner. If a diagram reads differently below L3, that itself is a signal worth questioning.
The conventions are defined on the color grammar and the line semantics; the worked trace is from diagnostics to decision.

title: L7 — Ecosystem & Strategy
lede: The top layer: grid, supply-chain, maintenance, and regulatory integration through a unified API, setting the intent that descends through the stack.
body: L7 Ecosystem & Strategy is where the plant meets everything outside it. It integrates grid dispatch, supply chains, maintenance planning, and regulatory constraints through a unified API layer, and it sets the plant-level intent that the stepped hierarchy carries down toward control.
Grid synchronization and dispatch scheduling for the plant's output.
Regulatory and safety-case constraints that bound the layers below.
Fleet coordination across breeder and burner units.

L7 is mostly purple (governance) and green (operations). It sets intent and constraints; it does not actuate. A dispatch window or a maintenance goal is passed to L5 copilots to translate into engineering objectives, then validated at L4 before anything reaches control. L7's authority is real but always mediated by the layers beneath it.

L7 reasons about timing, availability, and logistics — when to bring a unit up, when to schedule inspection, how to sequence fuel handling. It does not reason about price, cost, or value; those are outside the architecture entirely. The operations copilot at L5 shares this discipline.

L7 presents a single API to the outside world rather than a patchwork of subsystem interfaces. Grid operators, supply-chain systems, maintenance planners, and regulators each interact through governed endpoints, and every external request is subject to the same authority and audit rules as an internal one. This keeps the plant's boundary small and inspectable: there is one place where external intent enters, one place where it is validated, and one lineage record of what it asked for and what the plant did in response.
L7's intent descends through the stepped hierarchy; its constraints are enforced by the safety hierarchy and recorded by governance.

title: Architecture Glossary
lede: Concise definitions of the terms used across the AI-native architecture — layers, colors, lines, mechanisms, and machine physics.
body: This glossary defines the vocabulary of the Master Blueprint. Terms link to their full pages where one exists.
AI-native — intelligence designed into the plant from the first block diagram, not retrofit.
Layer (L0-L7) — a band of the stack holding a single latency and safety class.
Stepped hierarchy — the descent of authority from L7 strategy to L1 actuation.
Interface contract — the explicit, testable promise between adjacent layers.
Latency gradient — the monotone tightening of time budgets toward the hardware.
Color grammar — purple governance, blue infrastructure, green operations, yellow AI, orange reactor, pink feedback, gray framing.
Line semantics — microsecond real-time, standard telemetry, and offline batch classes.
IT/OT boundary — the gray line separating operational technology from general IT.
Autonomous hardware failsafe — deterministic quench dump with zero AI dependency.
Sub-10-microsecond boundary — the hard timing contract for safety-critical commands.
KRONOS-CTRL twin — the modular predictive twin (Power, Neutronics, Thermomechanics, MHD) running a 50-100 ms shadow.
PINN / GNN — physics-informed and graph neural networks used at L3.
MPC — model-predictive control planning bounded actuation over the twin.
Breeder (Hyperion) — D-T spherical tokamak; Q_sci 3.424, 88.7 MW, 9.86 MA, 16.84 T peak, delta -0.30; TBR lever 1.1/1.5/1.8.
Burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) — D-3He tandem mirror; 26.49 T plug, 17 T throat, 5.44% neutron fraction; direct energy conversion.
Ambipolar potential — the electrostatic confinement mechanism of the tandem mirror.
Negative triangularity — the breeder's ELM-suppressing plasma shape.
